tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__list_triggers
tools.description: List Routines (scheduled triggers) owned by this account. Use it to find trigger IDs (trig_...) for update_trigger and delete_trigger. From a thread in a Slack channel, only Routines that fire into that thread's session are listed unless all_in_channel is true. Each entry has the Routine's id, name, cron_expression, run_once_at, enabled state, ended_reason, next_run_at, created_at, persistent_session_id, and last_run. last_run is the most recent recorded run {status, fired_at, finished_at, session_id}. It is absent when no run was recorded (e.g. never fired). For a Routine that wakes an existing session, last_run records that the wake was delivered (SUCCEEDED) or failed to deliver, not how the turn went, unless run tracking covers that session. A FAILED or repeatedly non-SUCCEEDED last_run means the Routine is not doing its job. ended_reason says why a disabled Routine is permanently disabled. suspension_reason (e.g. subscription_paused) marks a temporary hold that lifts when the owner's subscription resumes. Both empty means user-paused. One-shot Routines that already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project are hidden unless include_completed is true. Scheduled tasks stored locally by the Cowork desktop app are not listed.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__read_documentation
tools.description: The documentation for the machine and product this session runs in: a claude.ai cloud container and the settings around it (GitHub access, connectors, the environment's secrets, network access, setup script and installed tools, the session's limits, Remote Control). Read it whenever something about your container or environment comes up, whether it blocked you, you worked around it, or the person asked how to set it up. For example: the repository the work is about is not in your container, a clone or push is refused, a service you need has no connected connector, an outbound host is denied, a command-line tool is missing, you need an API key. Read it rather than answering from memory because these settings move and get renamed faster than your training data, and a page says what is true now: the current steps, where in the product the person makes the change, and what you can do yourself. Reading a page also helps the person directly: in the Claude Code app they see a card with a button that takes them to that settings page, so they can fix it themselves while you carry on. Call it with no topic to list the pages and when each applies; call it with a topic to read that page. Read a page each time a different topic comes up; one read per topic is enough. It is read-only and needs no approval. It has nothing on bugs in the code you are working on.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a repo: mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to adopt or set up Claudinite, or to re-vendor a repo's mount.
- adopt-pack: Add packs to a repo already running Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable or declare a pack.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- backfilling-provenance: Filling a pack's empty provenance files from its history. Use when a pack carries empty provenance files, or when asked to backfill a pack's provenance.
- bug-investigation: Pinning down a bug's root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce.
- changing-pack-elements: What a change to a pack's element owes: the provenance entry, its kind, what a README carries. Loaded for any edit of a pack's rules, skills, checks, tasks or manifest.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Finding where a repo's CI time goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, on a runtime regression, or on a ci-performance finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut: one concern per commit, the issue it references, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made after the work in flight, as an issue queued behind it. Use on "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or any deferred change.
- extract-from-instructions: Convert instruction prose somebody already wrote into pack carriers. Use when adopting Claudinite on a repo with a CLAUDE.md, or when asked to convert instruction prose into a pack.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or file from the web: exact bytes over a summary, and what a 403 or egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl.
- file-placement: Where a file should live: the reference-distance metric and its exemptions. Use before placing, moving or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the basics task lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees. Use when adding, changing, explaining or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a technology nobody there has used yet. Use when asked to host, send or publish through something new, or to research it and create a skill.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner approves the current branch or PR, or asks to merge or land it into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back once a larger element has lived in production. Use when designing such an element, or when its merge completes it.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose for always-testable rules never converted to checks, and convert the strongest. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, or over prose a growth run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- running-the-suite: Running this repo's test suite: the one command that covers it, and reading a run's output from a file. Use before any node --test.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a merged change can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own. Use right after the merge.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a generated file: naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, resolving conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus: SKILL.md conventions, where its checks and tests live, pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a canon pack's skills/<name>/.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a person will execute. Use when filing or editing an issue that asks a human to click, set, register or copy something.
- writing-migration-plans: How a plan's phases are ordered so nothing stalls mid-run. Use before writing any DESIGN.md, migration, rollout or phased plan, or when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written: brevity, structure, triggerability, the provenance marker, a pack's pitch. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md, SKILL.md or manifest, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a repo-scanning check picks its files, strips comments, and proves itself silent on real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. * Pack versions are cut on main by automation, never in the pull request

A change under packs/<id>/ no longer bumps that pack's version itself. The
canon-curation pack gains pack-version-bump: a worker that walks the base
branch to each pack's last bump, cuts today's next version for every pack
with a shipping change since, and commits the manifests straight onto main
with git plumbing. The canon's pack-versions.yml workflow runs it on every
push to main; the task runs it daily for the merges a GITHUB_TOKEN push never
turns into a run.

pack-version-bumped and pack-version-claimed-once are removed with every
instruction to bump by hand or write a VERSIONS.md row. VERSIONS.md becomes
a derived record: the weekly pack-version-history task retraces from git
which pull requests each version shipped and appends the missing rows on a
self-landing pull request whose policy covers only those files.

Closes #1723
Closes #1689

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_017ATsfBUuAmhuRZH8mMYZYq

The record's comment claimed the engine reaches a member on its own release
cadence, so the gate would open only after a release cut. That is not how a
converge works: it clones canon HEAD and replaces the engine subtree wholesale
whatever ENGINE_VERSION says, and the engine flow runs before the pack flow so
packs are never checked against yesterday's engine. The op is therefore present
on the same converge that delivers the record.

Which is the cycle that matters, because it is the only one: pack-update stamps
the pack at its manifest version in the same run that applies its records, so a
cycle where the gate read false would put the record out of range for good.

Refs #1681

* Absorb barriers into basics, and stop it interviewing on adoption

`barriers` was not a pack anyone chose. It carried no fingerprint, and three
canon packs pulled it in via `requires` — one of them `claudinite-lifecycle`,
which `basics` requires — so it was already active in every member that declares
the baseline. That separate identity bought a second catalog row, a second
VERSIONS.md, a second badge, and an adoption question fired at owners who never
adopted anything.

The `barrier` check, the pack-contribution seam and the guide move into `basics`
(worldRules/barrier.mjs, barriers.mjs, barriers.md). A repo's graph moves to
`config.barriers.rules` on its `basics` entry; the check keeps a legacy read of
the old placement for the window between a member's mount converging and its
declaration doing so, retired by #1682. `RENAMED_PACKS` gains `barriers: basics`,
so a member declaring the old id activates the survivor rather than nothing, and
`legacy-shape-in-use` already names that entry in the holder's own findings.

The three `requires: ['barriers']` all go: every one of those walls became a
declared `forbidReferences` check the engine runs, so none of them needed a
second pack declared beside it — and `claudinite-lifecycle` could not have
pointed at `basics` anyway, which requires it back.

A new record converges the declaration. `absorbedPackConfig` is what a plain id
rename cannot do: two flat `config` objects spread over each other, so the
absorbed graph would land under the survivor's own key namespace, and an answer
recorded against a retired question would outlive it. The record is gated on the
member's own mount carrying the op, since the engine reaches a member on its own
release cadence — an engine without it would rename the id and leave the graph
where nothing reads it. Merging also stops leaving an absorbed pack's `via`
naming the survivor, which read as basics being required by basics.

Closes #1681

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01ESaQXhj7aNRbft9rgsjNDY

* Re-read the barriers absorption against the skills its files are scoped to

`writing-tests`, `writing-pack-prose` and `writing-claudinite-skills` are
force-loaded for the files this change touches, and were loaded after the fact.
Three things they caught:

The local pack's new rule about what a core file may name is rationale, not a
rule — the `barrier` check already enforces the boundary, and the part the check
cannot see (why `engine/migrations/` is deliberately outside the graph) is a
reason a review needs, not something a session acts on. It moves to the local
pack's references.md as (RULES-69), cited by the standing decision that was
already there, and the rule stays one sentence.

`assert.equal(pack.requires, undefined)` in product-wiki's manifest test pinned
a declaration to itself: it can only fail when someone changes the manifest on
purpose, which is not a defect. Removed rather than inverted — the assertion it
replaced had the same flaw.

Every new assertion was then made to bite: weakening the config stand-down, the
mount-capability probe and the config nesting each turns its own test red.

Refs #1681

The record's comment claimed the engine reaches a member on its own release
cadence, so the gate would open only after a release cut. That is not how a
converge works: it clones canon HEAD and replaces the engine subtree wholesale
whatever ENGINE_VERSION says, and the engine flow runs before the pack flow so
packs are never checked against yesterday's engine. The op is therefore present
on the same converge that delivers the record.

Which is the cycle that matters, because it is the only one: pack-update stamps
the pack at its manifest version in the same run that applies its records, so a
cycle where the gate read false would put the record out of range for good.

Refs #1681

expected_outcome grows from the two-word ceiling (none/pr) to four words
that also carry the target policy: no_code_changes, fresh_pr,
amend_existing_or_create_new_pr, supersede_existing_pr. The retired
none/pr normalize at the door beside open-pr/merged-pr, both declaration
checks advise the rename, and the schema and verifier follow.

queue/target.mjs resolves the branch and pull request between the
precondition's go and code-work: a task's open pull requests are
recognised by the claudinite/<pack>/<task>/ prefix or the Claudinite-Task:
trailer on the head commit; an amend reads the newest one's mergeability;
a supersede judges it by the runs on its head, landing a green incumbent
(the occurrence ends there) and closing the rest once the run's own pull
request exists. Code-work reads it as CLAUDINITE_TARGET_MODE/_BRANCH/_PR,
the agent as Target-branch:/Target-pr:/Supersedes: fields stamped at the
hand-off, and the session's converge performs the supersede closes when
handed --pr.

deliverGenerated takes the target as branch/pr and the update worker
pushes to the branch it is handed; each keeps its own discovery only
under an executor that predates the hand-off, marked for #1698.

By owner decision (2026-09-04) nine tasks change behaviour:
prose-to-checks-sweep, growth-extract, wiki-growth, improve-comments,
ci-performance, growth-discover-packs and growth-promote amend their open
pull request; rule-revalidation and growth-dedup supersede theirs. Their
task.md files deliver on the branch and pull request the item names,
wiki-growth's no-open-pr-touching precondition retires, a discovery run
authors one pack per run, and a promote run names a technology with no
home on its tracker rather than minting the stub in a second pull
request. update declares supersede_existing_pr and usage-fold
amend_existing_or_create_new_pr, what each already did.

tasks-dispatch DESIGN gains step 4b and decision 15.32; the lane
documents and writing-tasks follow; every touched pack is bumped.

* Absorb barriers into basics, and stop it interviewing on adoption

`barriers` was not a pack anyone chose. It carried no fingerprint, and three
canon packs pulled it in via `requires` — one of them `claudinite-lifecycle`,
which `basics` requires — so it was already active in every member that declares
the baseline. That separate identity bought a second catalog row, a second
VERSIONS.md, a second badge, and an adoption question fired at owners who never
adopted anything.

The `barrier` check, the pack-contribution seam and the guide move into `basics`
(worldRules/barrier.mjs, barriers.mjs, barriers.md). A repo's graph moves to
`config.barriers.rules` on its `basics` entry; the check keeps a legacy read of
the old placement for the window between a member's mount converging and its
declaration doing so, retired by #1682. `RENAMED_PACKS` gains `barriers: basics`,
so a member declaring the old id activates the survivor rather than nothing, and
`legacy-shape-in-use` already names that entry in the holder's own findings.

The three `requires: ['barriers']` all go: every one of those walls became a
declared `forbidReferences` check the engine runs, so none of them needed a
second pack declared beside it — and `claudinite-lifecycle` could not have
pointed at `basics` anyway, which requires it back.

A new record converges the declaration. `absorbedPackConfig` is what a plain id
rename cannot do: two flat `config` objects spread over each other, so the
absorbed graph would land under the survivor's own key namespace, and an answer
recorded against a retired question would outlive it. The record is gated on the
member's own mount carrying the op, since the engine reaches a member on its own
release cadence — an engine without it would rename the id and leave the graph
where nothing reads it. Merging also stops leaving an absorbed pack's `via`
naming the survivor, which read as basics being required by basics.

Closes #1681

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01ESaQXhj7aNRbft9rgsjNDY

* Re-read the barriers absorption against the skills its files are scoped to

`writing-tests`, `writing-pack-prose` and `writing-claudinite-skills` are
force-loaded for the files this change touches, and were loaded after the fact.
Three things they caught:

The local pack's new rule about what a core file may name is rationale, not a
rule — the `barrier` check already enforces the boundary, and the part the check
cannot see (why `engine/migrations/` is deliberately outside the graph) is a
reason a review needs, not something a session acts on. It moves to the local
pack's references.md as (RULES-69), cited by the standing decision that was
already there, and the rule stays one sentence.

`assert.equal(pack.requires, undefined)` in product-wiki's manifest test pinned
a declaration to itself: it can only fail when someone changes the manifest on
purpose, which is not a defect. Removed rather than inverted — the assertion it
replaced had the same flaw.

Every new assertion was then made to bite: weakening the config stand-down, the
mount-capability probe and the config nesting each turns its own test red.

Refs #1681

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01ESaQXhj7aNRbft9rgsjNDY

* Point the relocated segregation rule at the graph's new home

#1674 moved the packs/-tree segregation rule out of the canon home's local
pack and into claudinite-canon-curation, where it still named the barriers
pack. The canon's own reason for its graph — retired from that pack's
adoption answer — goes with the rule, as (RULES-12) rather than a second
local-pack entry nothing cites.

Refs #1681

Every corpus rule classified by the moment that could carry it — world,
work, action, trigger — and the end-state design of the vocabulary those
moments need: two-pass derive→assert sets, declarative work assertions,
declared action guards, and skill triggers beyond file edits.

* Declared checks: pass two — value sets from lines and paths, quantified

extractValueSets derives from lines (fromLinesMatching + inFilesMatching,
splitValuesOn), tracked paths, added lines (work scope) and fanned-out
parsed fields (valuesAtFields), each value carrying its origin and the
named groups that found it; whenSetEmpty may report the empty set.
checkSetValues quantifies a set against the tree (some file matches a
filled template / none does / a path exists / a tracked path matches),
checkSetPairs joins two sets, requireIdenticalFiles holds twins equal.
Line-derived sets fill during the shared sweep through collectors, so a
two-pass rule still costs one walk.

{"total_count":691,"workflow_runs":[{"id":36449078746,"name":"CI","display_title":"Pack manifests become pack.json (#2382)","workflow_id":317526095,"run_number":2534,"run_attempt":1,"event":"push","status":"completed","conclusion":"success","head_branch":"main","head_sha":"4216d7d0946df15026c629a7679e21f5b2a47716","head_commit":{"message":"Pack manifests become pack.json (#2382)

* Read pack.json manifests, preferring them over pack.mjs

A pack directory is a pack when it carries pack.json or pack.mjs, and where
it carries both the JSON wins. The loader parses a pack.json with no import;
the three things JSON cannot spell get a form of their own:

- a relevanceDetector pattern is its source string or { source, flags },
  compiled at load for either manifest spelling;
- a templated env setup/probe is { forEach, whenUnset, template }, repeated
  per value of one of the pack entry's config params;
- the contributedRules seam is a contributed-rules.mjs beside the manifest.

Every reader that finds, names or scrapes a manifest now takes either
spelling: the version bump and its history walk, the provenance tooling and
its change check, the dashboard's and the fleet roster's version reads, the
seed sweep's vendored probe, the checks that select manifests by path, and
the personal-pack copier and local-pack seed, which now write pack.json.
The manifest names live in pack-conventions.mjs, read by packs through a
namespace with a pack.mjs-only fallback for an older engine.

A rehearsal fixture proves a member's local pack.json converges green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Migrate members' local pack.mjs manifests to pack.json

A new named codemod, manifestsToJson, evaluates each local pack's pack.mjs
and writes its default export back as pack.json, key order kept and each
relevanceDetector pattern as its source string or { source, flags }. A
manifest JSON cannot carry - a function, a module importing a sibling -
stays a module, which the loader still reads, and the run says why.

The pack-json-manifests record runs it at engine 60928.1, gated on the
member's mount carrying an engine that reads pack.json, since an older one
would discover no pack in a directory holding only that file. The same
conversion has a CLI for converting a checkout by hand.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Take the code out of the basics and node manifests

The two manifests holding a function now hold only data. basics'
contributedRules seam moves to contributed-rules.mjs beside the manifest,
which the loader finds by name. node's env setup and probe become
{ forEach: 'dirs', whenUnset: ['.'], template } values, rendering the same
commands the functions built for an unset, empty or listed config.dirs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Inline the values four manifests imported, and guard them against drift

github-pages, product-wiki, public-website and claudinite-fleet-sheepdog
each built a manifest value from another module: the site config and
deploy-workflow paths, the wiki's sink README, the page's version stamp,
and the fleet token's adoption step. Each is now written out in the
manifest, and the pack's own test runs the real module against it - the
lib's paths are found by the fingerprint, the stamp's source matches, the
rendered handover step deep-equals the manifest's - so a change on either
side goes red. The tests load each pack through the registry, so they hold
whichever manifest spelling the pack carries.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Write the fingerprints' patterns as strings

Every relevanceDetector pattern in a canon manifest is now its source
string, or { source, flags } where it carries a flag - the form a
pack.json holds, which the loader compiles back into a RegExp. Escaped
slashes are dropped, since a source string needs none. Every pack's loaded
manifest hashes identically before and after, patterns' sources and flags
included.

The tests that imported a pack.mjs to read its fingerprint now load the
pack through the registry, which is what compiles the strings and what
reads either manifest spelling.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Take the comments out of the pack manifests

A manifest that is data carries no comments, so every pack.mjs loses its
own ahead of the conversion. Most described the pack, which its README and
pitch already say, and are gone. The ones recording a decision - why a pack
is hidden or never fingerprinted, why it requires another, why an adoption
step is a handover, why a fingerprint reads as it does - are now an entry
on that pack's provenance/_pack.md. The one piece of usage no README held,
node's config.dirs, is now in the node README. Every pack loads
identically before and after.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Convert every pack manifest to pack.json

Every canon pack and this repo's own local pack now carries a pack.json,
written by the migration's converter from each module's evaluated export,
and no pack.mjs. Each pack loads identically before and after. Every canon
pack's minEngineVersion moves to 60928.1, the first engine that reads the
JSON manifest: an older one would find no pack in these directories.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Release engine 60928.1

The first engine that reads a pack.json manifest. Every canon pack now
requires it, and the pack-json-manifests record ranges against it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Record the canary run that qualified engine 60928.1

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Rework the fingerprints review found weak

product-wiki, public-website and executable-requirements lose their
fingerprints: each matched the pack's own artifact or one project's layout,
never a sign a repo would want the pack, so all three are declared by hand.

headless-browser and jwt now read a near-root package.json,
requirements*.txt or pyproject.toml for the driver or JWT library they
declare, rather than every source file that uses one; a usage no manifest
backs, a name in prose and a lookalike package do not fire.

chrome-extension fires only on a manifest.json at the root or one
directory down declaring "manifest_version": 3, so an MV2 extension and a
fixture deep in the tree no longer do.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Retire pack contributions

No pack contributed a barrier, so the contributedRules seam built nothing.
The engine calls no seam any more, and basics' contributed-rules.mjs and
barriers.mjs are deleted; the barrier rule names its doc itself. A pack's
fixed barrier is a declared forbidReferences check, and a repo's own is
config.barriers.rules on its basics entry.

The spec still accepts `contributes` and `contributedRules` for one
convergence window, since a member's own local pack may carry either and
an unknown field would block its checks. legacy-shape-in-use names each
local manifest still carrying one, and #2395 removes the tolerance.

Refs #2395

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Record the canary run over the final 60928.1 tree

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01T1M31sY1mGiN3g8UXDdSU4

* Retire pack contributions

No pack contributed a barrier, so the contributedRules seam built nothing.
The engine calls no seam any more, and basics' contributed-rules.mjs and
barriers.mjs are deleted; the barrier rule names its doc itself. A pack's
fixed barrier is a declared forbidReferences check, and a repo's own is
config.barriers.rules on its basics entry.

The spec still accepts `contributes` and `contributedRules` for one
convergence window, since a member's own local pack may carry either and
an unknown field would block its checks. legacy-shape-in-use names each
local manifest still carrying one, and #2395 removes the tolerance.

Yes, it's working. Every updated member I checked loads its packs on the new engine, and I found no failure caused by the change.

**Canon:** CI passed on the merge commit (run 36449078746).

**Fleet:** I cloned each member and loaded its packs with its own engine copy, then ran its world checks. I couldn't clone about a dozen names Shepherd references (hitbut, A, WIP and others); those are probably private, so I couldn't check them.

| Member | Engine | Local manifest | Packs load | World checks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shepherd | 60928.1 | converted to `pack.json` | 8 | pass; Checks CI green after update PR #808 |
| CrosswordChat | 60928.1 | converted to `pack.json` | 12 | 2 blocking findings, both there before the update |
| TLDR | 60928.1 | stays `pack.mjs` | 10 | pass |
| GoogleCalendarEventCreator | 60928.1 | stays `pack.mjs` | 11 | 37 blocking findings, all there before the update |
| VascularColoring | 60928.1 | stays `pack.mjs` | 7 | pass |
| ClaudiniteCanary | 60928.1 | stays `pack.mjs` | 8 | pass |
| EdFringeNow | 60927.1 | stays `pack.mjs` | 12 | pass |

- **Why four stay `pack.mjs`:** their manifests import their own coded checks, which a JSON file can't hold, so the migration leaves them as modules by design. The loader still reads them, and every one loaded.
- **The two failing members:** I checked out each one's commit just before the update and ran the same checks there. The findings were the same kinds (`cer/release-workflows`, `claudinite-isolation`), all there before the update.
- **EdFringeNow:** it's one release behind, and its next nightly update should bring it to 60928.1.
- **One advisory per member:** each still carries an old `detect` field that nothing reads any more. That's an old leftover, not from this change, and it's advisory only.

> ✅ All done

attachment.content:
- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a repo: mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to adopt or set up Claudinite, or to re-vendor a repo's mount.
- adopt-pack: Add packs to a repo already running Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable or declare a pack.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- backfilling-provenance: Filling a pack's empty provenance files from its history. Use when a pack carries empty provenance files, or when asked to backfill a pack's provenance.
- bug-investigation: Pinning down a bug's root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce.
- changing-pack-elements: What a change to a pack's element owes: the provenance entry, its kind, what a README carries. Loaded for any edit of a pack's rules, skills, checks, tasks or manifest.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Finding where a repo's CI time goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, on a runtime regression, or on a ci-performance finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut: one concern per commit, the issue it references, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made after the work in flight, as an issue queued behind it. Use on "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or any deferred change.
- extract-from-instructions: Convert instruction prose somebody already wrote into pack carriers. Use when adopting Claudinite on a repo with a CLAUDE.md, or when asked to convert instruction prose into a pack.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or file from the web: exact bytes over a summary, and what a 403 or egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl.
- file-placement: Where a file should live: the reference-distance metric and its exemptions. Use before placing, moving or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the basics task lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees. Use when adding, changing, explaining or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a technology nobody there has used yet. Use when asked to host, send or publish through something new, or to research it and create a skill.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner approves the current branch or PR, or asks to merge or land it into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back once a larger element has lived in production. Use when designing such an element, or when its merge completes it.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose for always-testable rules never converted to checks, and convert the strongest. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, or over prose a growth run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- running-the-suite: Running this repo's test suite: the one command that covers it, and reading a run's output from a file. Use before any node --test.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a merged change can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own. Use right after the merge.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a generated file: naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, resolving conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus: SKILL.md conventions, where its checks and tests live, pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a canon pack's skills/<name>/.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a person will execute. Use when filing or editing an issue that asks a human to click, set, register or copy something.
- writing-migration-plans: How a plan's phases are ordered so nothing stalls mid-run. Use before writing any DESIGN.md, migration, rollout or phased plan, or when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written: brevity, structure, triggerability, the provenance marker, a pack's pitch. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md, SKILL.md or manifest, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a repo-scanning check picks its files, strips comments, and proves itself silent on real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/committing

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking. (concern-commit)
- **Reference the issue, when the change has one** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where
  the commit finishes it. A change tracked by its PR alone references nothing.
  (reference-issue-change)
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
  (landed-commit-revised)
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress. (stage-name)

content.text: The two files are empty. The `changing-pack-elements` skill says what kind of entry a move like this gets, so I'll load it before writing one.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/changing-pack-elements

# Changing a pack's elements

A pack's carriers - the rules in `RULES.md`, a skill and its triggers, a coded or declared
check, a task and its policy, the manifest - say *what* a session does. The decision behind
each - why it reads so, who decided, from what evidence, why this carrier and this trigger,
what was rejected, what would retire it - is one append-only file per element under the
pack's `provenance/`, read by maintenance and never by a session. Three things follow for
any edit under a pack.

## 1. The edit owes an entry, in the same change

Every change to what a carrier decides lands with an entry on the element's file, and the
`provenance-change-recorded` check says so again at the Stop hook when it did not. Which
file: the marker that ends a rule or guideline names it (`(url-filter-host-operators)` →
`provenance/url-filter-host-operators.md`), and two carriers may name one file while their
history is one; an unmarked guideline's is its skill's; a skill's is its directory name; a
check's its id with `/` as `-`; a task's its id; the manifest's `_pack.md`. Which kind:

| The change | Kind |
|---|---|
| a rule, guideline, skill body or step reads differently | `reworded` - or `strengthened` / `weakened` when the modality moved |
| a rule split in two, or two folded into one | `split` / `merged` (an entry on every file involved) |
| a guideline given a file of its own, its history having diverged from its skill's | `split` on the skill's file, `born` on the bullet's, with `Mechanism` |
| a rule moved to another carrier or pack | `moved`, with `Mechanism` |
| prose turned into a check | `converted`, with `Mechanism` and the deletion-test verdict |
| a skill's description or `force-load-on-*` trigger | `trigger-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a task's preconditions, `expected_outcome`, `automerge`, model or worker | `policy-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a check's `on_fail`, or the gate deciding when it fires | `severity-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| what an element applies to, where its text reads the same - a manifest's `requires` or fingerprint, a check's file scope, a skill's corpus | `scope-changed`, with `Mechanism` |
| a new element | `born`, with `Mechanism` - and `mark` first if the carrier has no file |
| an element removed | `retired` - the file stays, and this is its last entry |
| a review that found new evidence or changed the retire test | `reaffirmed`; a review that found nothing new writes nothing |

No entry is owed for whitespace, a re-wrap, a code comment in a check, a fixture, a test, a
README row, a version bump, or the marking pass's own markers and `body:` lines.

Write the entry in the file grammar and append it through the tool, which validates it and
refuses one that carries a secret:

```
node packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs append <pack> <element> <<'EOF'
## 2026-09-21 · reworded · the consequence clause said why twice (#2210)
- **Reason:** the second sentence restated the rule; cut.
- **Actor:** @handle (owner).
- **Model:** <the model this session runs, as the harness names it>
- **Landed:** #2210
EOF
```

In a member the tool is `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/provenance.mjs`, and
the pack is under `.claudinite/local/packs/`. `--changed` in place of the element appends the
same entry to every element the working tree's diff touched - a sweep's one-line entries.
The fields, each written only where there is something behind it: `Source`, `Reason`,
`Actor` (the person by handle with their role, or the run and who merged it - never an
email), `Model`, `Mechanism` (the carrier and its trigger, and why - required on `born`,
`converted`, `moved`, `trigger-changed`, `policy-changed`, `severity-changed`), `Rejected`,
`Retire when`, `Landed`. An entry never restates the rule: the carrier is the description,
the entry is the decision. A candidate turned down goes on `_declined.md` the same way, kind
`declined`, with `Source`, `Reason` and `Actor`.

**Size the entry to the decision, never to the work.** Most are three to five lines. Each
field is the shortest answer that is still an answer, and one clause is usually the whole of
one - `Reason: the folder never existed.` Where a required `Mechanism` keeps the carrier it
already had, the new value is the whole of it - `a regex` - and the why-clause is owed only
where the choice of carrier was itself the decision. The diff, the commit message and the
pull request already hold what changed, how it was proved and what it cost; an entry
retelling any of them writes the record twice and buries the line a review came for. Length
is earned only by a decision that was weighed - an alternative turned down, a constraint that
forced the shape - so a corrected path, a repointed pattern or a renamed field gets one line,
and a change nobody deliberated over gets `Reason` alone. Cut a field rather than pad it, and
cut one that repeats another field or the entry's own title.

A file is meant to grow: a wrong entry is answered by a later one, never by editing the one
that was wrong. The check advises against a line lost or altered and refuses nothing.

### The one lane that writes the past

`append` and `apply` are append-only, and the tool enforces it: an entry dated before the
file's last is refused, because a change being recorded now cannot have happened before the
change recorded last. **The backfill is the deliberate exception**, and `--backfill` on
either command is how it says so. It is deriving a history that already happened, so its
entries are dated in the past by definition, and under that flag the file is re-rendered in
date order rather than appended to. Two things only it may do:

- **Replace what the references conversion wrote.** A file the conversion filled carries a
  `born` dated by the conversion write rather than by the element. Where the batch brings a
  born dated on or before it - an earlier birth, or the same day verified with the commit
  behind it - that placeholder is what is being corrected and the tool drops it, naming it
  in the run's output; a batch bringing no born leaves it standing. The dates decide, so
  neither truncating these files as a class nor leaving them is the rule. Only the
  conversion's own entry is ever replaced - an entry somebody wrote is never dropped,
  whatever its date.
- **Open a file the marking pass could not.** An element retired *before* that pass is named
  by no carrier, so nothing will ever create its file. A `--backfill` batch that opens with
  `born` creates it; its whole history, birth through `retired`, arrives at once or not at
  all. Do not put such a history on `_pack.md` instead: a `retired` entry seals the file it
  ends, and `_pack.md` is the one file in a pack that must stay appendable forever.

Every other caller - every change being made now - uses the plain lane, where a file only
ever grows at its end.

## 2. The README carries use, never history

A pack's `README.md` is for the person adopting the pack or reaching for one of its
elements: when the pack activates, what each check demands and what satisfies it, when a
skill is the thing to load, what the task does to the repository, and the catalog of what
the pack carries. Never how an element came to be, what it replaced, why its id reads as it
does, what an earlier shape did, or how the pack is maintained. The test is the sentence: a
date, a pull request number, an "until", a "was", a "kept as it was" or a "distilled from"
is a decision, and a decision is an entry on the element's file - `_pack.md` for the pack's
own shape. Move it there; do not write it here.

## 3. The mount is never edited

A file under `.claudinite/shared/` arrived from a canon and the next update replaces the
whole tree. Change it in the canon, or carry the difference in the repo's own
`.claudinite/local/packs/`.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-pack-prose

# Writing pack prose

Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.

**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.

## The ration

Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.

- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet. (sentence-rule-near)
- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real. (extraction-pass-adds)
- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
  trigger. (split-rule-carries)
- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs on the element's
  provenance file (below). (skill-md-loads)
- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads. (moving-rule-out)
- **Starting a `SKILL.md`, or editing one that declares no body** — say under its frontmatter
  `metadata` what the body is: `body: workflow` for a procedure, whose steps and their gotchas
  change as one, or `body: guidelines` for rules behind a trigger, kept on the skill's one file
  until one has a history of its own. A skill that mixes the two declares the shape of its
  greater part. The harness ignores the key; the corpus's own maintenance reads it, and never
  infers it. (starting-skill-md)

## Shape a rule so it fires

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it. (keying-rule-trigger)
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
  (keying-rule-reader)
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
  (keying-rule-corrects)
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
  (phrasing-trigger)
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets. (choosing-unit)
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
  (splitting-rule-only)
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
  (separating-blocks)
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would. (ordering-file-many)
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change. (grouping-separates-rules)
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
  (ordering-clauses)
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it. (choosing-modality)
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
  (naming-mechanism)
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command. (telling-reader-run)
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces. (closing-block)
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding. (keeping-exception)
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
  reader doesn't need at act time goes on the element's provenance file (below).
  (cutting-rules-prose)
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find. (auditing-file-rules)
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either. (rewriting-existing-rule)

## A pack's pitch

- **Knowing who reads a pitch** - a developer whose repository does not run Claudinite, deciding
  from this one paragraph on the claudinite.com dashboard whether the pack is worth adopting. No
  session ever loads it, so it sells the pack rather than instructing anyone.

- **Writing a pitch** - lead with what goes wrong in a repository without the pack, then what
  the pack changes: its main skills by name and the process it runs by itself. Plain and
  concrete, with no hype, no commands, no markdown, no links and no paths, inside the manifest's
  word cap.

- **Counting what a pack carries in its pitch** - in rounded words ("a few", "about a dozen",
  "dozens"), only for the kinds the pack has, never an exact number: the pitch then survives the
  pack's growth, and is rewritten only when what the pack is for changes.

- **Pitching a stub pack** - say it starts empty and is where the repository's own lessons
  about its subject collect; never promise content it does not carry.

## The provenance log - where a rule's rationale lives

A pack keeps one file per element under `provenance/`, beside its `RULES.md`: an append-only
log of the decisions behind the element, read by maintenance and review - the pass that asks
whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written - and never by a session.
No rule sends its reader there, nothing loads it, and it never vendors: a member mounting a
canon pack receives the rules, not the reasoning behind them. The grammar, the kinds, the
fields and the tool are [changing-pack-elements](../changing-pack-elements/SKILL.md)'s; what
this skill adds is how a rule is written so the log can hold it.

- **Ending a rule** - every rule in a `RULES.md` ends with the bare marker naming its file -
  `… never a filesystem walk. (url-filter-host-operators)` - and nothing else: don't name the
  folder, don't link it, don't ask the reader to follow anything. The marker is the element's
  id: two to four hyphenated words for the guideline rather than its wording, chosen once and
  never renamed, so a rewording never touches it and a member's override can name it. Two
  rules whose history is one may share a marker. A guidelines skill's bullets are the skill's
  file's and carry none, until one's history diverges and it takes a marker and a file of its
  own; a workflow skill's steps carry none, the skill being the element. (ending-rule)
- **Adding a rule** - write the brief rule and end it with its marker; create its file with a
  `born` entry through `provenance.mjs append` (`mark` creates the file where none exists),
  and put the reason there, never in the rule. A consequence the reader needs under pressure
  earns its clause; rationale the reader doesn't need at act time is the entry's. Write the
  entry so a future review can **reaffirm the rule from it** - `Retire when` is what would
  have to be true for the rule to go. (adding-rule)
  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    the error, the measured cost).
  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it - in a member's
    local pack; a canon file carries the paraphrase, never the quote.
- **Rewording, moving, splitting or converting a rule** - the entry is owed in the same
  change, and the forced skill names its kind. (rewording-moving-splitting)
- **A check's rationale** - on the check's own file, named by its id (`cer/version-bumped` →
  `cer-version-bumped.md`); nothing is added to the check. (checks-rationale)
- **Removing a rule or check** - its file stays and gains a `retired` entry as its last, in
  the same change. (removing-rule-check)

The `provenance-integrity` check holds the mechanism together - every carrier names a live
file, every file parses - and `provenance-change-recorded` holds the change: a carrier that
changed lands with its entry. A pack not yet on the convention is put there by
`provenance.mjs mark`, and its history filled by the
[backfilling-provenance](../backfilling-provenance/SKILL.md) skill; nothing here is done rule by
rule.

## Evidence

The commit and its PR remain the archive - the story of the incident, quoted exchanges and
session ids live there and in the capture, never in the rule and never in a canon's log. What

a future review needs to re-test the rule, and `Retire when`, the test it is reaffirmed
against. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument - a cost
the reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

input.head: claude/gifted-cori-limlre
input.title: Provenance reads const-declared check ids; the manifest converter drops detect and marker
input.body:
Two canon fixes surfaced while cleaning the members' local packs (their checks moved into `worldRules/` / `workRules/`, manifests to `pack.json`):

- **Provenance reads a `const id = '…'` exported by shorthand.** Member rule modules (GoogleCalendarEventCreator, ClaudiniteCanary) write `const id = '…'; export default { id, … }`. The helper matched only `id: '…'` literals, so once those checks sit in a rule folder their provenance files read as "named by no carrier" — an advisory with a grace period that turns blocking on 2026-10-04. A const counts only where an object takes it by shorthand.
- **The manifest converter drops the retired `detect`/`marker`.** Carrying them into a freshly written `pack.json` keeps `legacy-shape-in-use` firing on the file the conversion just wrote. The list sits in `pack-schema.mjs` beside the two fields, under the same `retire:#2374` tolerance.

Consumer safety: no manifest field changes. The `prose-only` rehearsal fixture already carries a local `pack.mjs` with `detect`/`marker`; I converged it in both modes and the update writes a `pack.json` without them. Its `why` now says so.

Tests: 4110/4110 pass; the rehearsal gate 82/82; both new tests seen red first.

Comment class: feature

I've cleaned all six local packs, with one PR per member plus one canon PR. Each pack's checks now sit in its `worldRules/` or `workRules/` folder, and its manifest is a `pack.json` holding only `ruleRoutingGuidance`. `detect` and `marker` are gone everywhere, including from the one pack already on `pack.json` (Shepherd).

**PRs:**
- [missingbulb/Shepherd#820](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/pull/820): manifest cleanup only, since it has no coded checks.
- [missingbulb/TLDR#651](https://github.com/missingbulb/TLDR/pull/651)
- [missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator#1384](https://github.com/missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator/pull/1384)
- [missingbulb/VascularColoring#554](https://github.com/missingbulb/VascularColoring/pull/554)
- [missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary#580](https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/pull/580)
- [missingbulb/EdFringeNow#963](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/963)
- [missingbulb/Claudinite#2403](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2403): two canon fixes the cleanup turned up.

**Verification:** each pack loads the same checks, skills and fields as before; only the order now follows the folder. In the canary, only `pack-shape`'s own wording changed, because I rewrote it. Each repo's pack tests and its world and Stop-hook checks show nothing new. Canon's suite passes all 4110 tests, and every test I added or rewrote failed before its fix went in.

**Changes beyond moving files:**
- **Canary:** its own checks enforced the old manifest layout. `pack-shape` now reads the folders instead of the manifest's lists, `pack-intact` requires `pack.json`, and its RULES.md bullet says the same.
- **EdFringeNow tests:** two tests imported `pack.mjs` to assert each check was listed. They now load the pack through the engine and assert each check is actually loaded.
- **EdFringeNow `doc:` fields:** five checks pointed at a bare `RULES.md`, which names no real file from the repo root. The move put them in view of the pointer check, so I fixed them in a separate commit.
- **Provenance:** each moved check got a provenance file, with its birth traced through git history and a `moved` entry.

**Canon fixes (#2403):**
- **Provenance helper:** it now recognises `const id = '…'` when an object exports it as `{ id, … }`. GoogleCalendarEventCreator and ClaudiniteCanary write their checks that way. Until #2403 merges and the nightly update delivers it, those two repos will show a "named by no carrier" advisory, which becomes blocking on 2026-10-04.
- **Converter:** when the update migration converts a manifest, it now drops `detect` and `marker`.

GoogleCalendarEventCreator's and ClaudiniteCanary's checks still spell `severity` instead of `on_fail`. That was already flagged before this change, and I left it alone as out of scope.
